drug_class: Vitamin D analog (active form of Vitamin D)
purpose: Calcitriol is used to treat low calcium levels and bone disease in people whose kidneys or parathyroid glands are not working properly. It is also used in patients on dialysis to help keep their bones strong and healthy. Doctors may also prescribe it for certain skin conditions like psoriasis in a topical form.
how_it_works: Your body normally turns vitamin D from food or sunlight into an active form that helps your gut absorb calcium from food. When your kidneys are not working well, they cannot make this active vitamin D on their own. Calcitriol is already in that active form, so it steps in and helps your body absorb and use calcium properly without needing healthy kidneys to process it.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, loss of appetite, headache, weakness, dry mouth, or constipation. Some people may feel unusually thirsty or need to urinate more often than normal.
warnings: Too much calcitriol can raise your calcium levels too high, which is dangerous and can affect your heart, kidneys, and muscles. Tell your doctor right away if you have muscle weakness, confusion, extreme thirst, bone pain, or irregular heartbeat. Avoid taking extra calcium or vitamin D supplements unless your doctor tells you it is okay. Let your doctor know about all other medications you take, especially antacids containing magnesium.
typical_dosing: The dose is very individual and depends on your condition and lab results. A common starting dose for adults is 0.25 micrograms taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on regular blood tests checking your calcium and other levels. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and never change your dose on your own.
